title: Cluster Analysis of Brain Activation Data Without Thresholds
author: Gladwin, Vink, et al.

steps.title: Prepare activation map
steps.instruction: Obtain a statistical activation map of –log(p) values derived from a T‑map or F‑map; use SPM toolbox functions in MATLAB for reading, saving, and (if needed) smoothing the data.

steps.title: Define clusters via recursive search
steps.instruction: Iteratively identify clusters by starting at the highest‑valued voxel and expanding outward with a recursive neighbor‑visiting algorithm that adds voxels only while the slope to the new voxel is more positive than the previous slope, then repeat after excluding already‑assigned voxels until no local maxima remain.

substeps.instruction: Select the voxel with the highest –log(p) value.
Recursively visit its neighboring voxels, then their neighbors, always moving farther from the peak voxel to avoid back‑tracking.
Add a neighboring voxel only if the slope (difference in value) from the previous voxel to the new voxel is more positive than the slope that led to the previous voxel.
Stop adding voxels when the slope condition fails; the set of visited voxels constitutes one cluster.
Exclude all voxels of the defined cluster from further processing.
Identify the next highest‑valued voxel among the remaining voxels and repeat the procedure.
Define a local maximum as any voxel whose eight neighboring voxels all have lower values.

steps.title: Combine adjacent clusters
steps.instruction: Merge neighboring clusters when a quantitative connection criterion is satisfied, using the proportion of edge voxels that touch another cluster and the relative peak heights.

substeps.instruction: For each cluster, calculate ProportionConnected = (number of edge voxels bordering a different cluster) / (total number of edge voxels).
If ProportionConnected > 0, compute PeaksDifference = |peak₁ – peak₂| (difference between the two clusters’ peak values).
Compute SmallerPeakToConnectingEdge = (peak of the lower‑peak cluster) – (mean activation of its edge voxels that touch the neighboring cluster).
Combine the two clusters if the inequality holds: PeaksDifference / (PeaksDifference + SmallerPeakToConnectingEdge) ≥ 1 – ProportionConnected.
Optionally, for speed a liberal voxel‑wise threshold of p = 0.05 may be applied before this step, though the method does not require any threshold.

steps.title: Assess significance with permutation testing
steps.instruction: Determine which clusters are statistically significant by building a null distribution of whole‑brain maximum cluster activation scores through sign‑flipping permutations.

substeps.instruction: For each permutation, independently multiply each subject’s data by –1 with probability 0.5 (sign‑flip) and leave it unchanged otherwise; this preserves spatial dependence while enforcing the null hypothesis.
Generate a permuted –log(p) activation map and define clusters using the same recursive‑search algorithm described above.
For each cluster, compute its activation score as the sum of the –log(p) values of all voxels in the cluster.
Record the maximum cluster activation score across the whole brain for that permutation.
Repeat for a sufficient number of permutations to obtain a stable null distribution of maximum scores.
Determine the activation‑score threshold that corresponds to the 5 % upper tail of the null distribution (i.e., fewer than 5 % of permutation maxima exceed this value).
In the original, non‑permuted map, declare any cluster whose activation score exceeds this threshold as significant at a 5 % false‑positive level.

steps.title: Generate significant cluster mask
steps.instruction: Create a binary mask containing all voxels belonging to significant clusters and save it using SPM toolbox functions; the algorithm implementation is available in the hiro3 fMRI visualization tool.

substeps.instruction: Collect voxels from all clusters that passed the permutation‑test threshold.
Create a binary image (mask) where these voxels are set to 1 and all others to 0.
Save the mask (and any accompanying statistics) with SPM’s file‑handling utilities.
